 Follow Angie Nixon Says Democrats Should Invest More In Florida And Stop Treating Black Voters As ‘A Sure Thing’
 Christopher Rhodes Mon, October 26, 2026 at 6:04 PM UTC 5 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. As the midterm elections quickly approach, Democrats hold onto their hopes of retaking the House of Representatives and perhaps even the Senate. But as Democrats seek to push their message and capitalize on discontent with the GOP, many within the party are calling out their fellow Democrats for ignoring Black voters and candidates in the South and across the country and limiting the party's prospects as a result.
 Angie Nixon calls out Democratic Party over limited support in Florida race and beyond
 "There needs to be a long conversation regarding the state of Black people within the Democratic Party," said Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon as she appeared on The Conversation , a podcast hosted by Politico's Dasha Burns. Nixon described frustration among Black voters concerning the party's attitude toward them. "Oftentimes they want our labor and not our leadership." Nixon, who is running an uphill Senate campaign in Florida, told Burns, "We want to make sure we're not only battling stuff outside of the party, or battling racism outside of the party, and then we want to make sure we're not battling it inside as well." Nixon also said she was not surprised that Democrats lost some of the Black vote in 2024. "We have to make sure we go out and talk to people year-round. We can't take anyone for granted." Because "Black people have historically been the backbone of the party," Nixon argues that the party has often taken Black voters for granted, with Democrats treating the Black vote "a sure thing."
 While Nixon pointed to neglect for Black voters and underinvestment in southern candidates, she rejected the idea that racism was playing a direct role in these decisions. Rather, Nixon argued that racism "may be playing a role in a sense that people are saying, 'Oh, I don't think she can win in the South because people are so racist.' And that is the level of it, right?" Nixon explained. "I don't think it's something nefarious or that people trying to, that Democratic donors are racist towards me. I would say it's that they think that the state is racist and they're just hesitant to donate because of it." Nixon also agreed that Democrats had made "a huge mistake" by not investing in Florida, allowing the state to become a "testing ground" for regressive policies like the state's anti-DEI initiatives that have later influenced policies on a national level. At the same time, Nixon argues that progressive initiatives have succeeded in Florida, such as raising the state's minimum wage and restoring rights for formerly incarcerated individuals. "And so we're winning on progressive issues, and the only thing is, we need to have the money to be able to communicate so that we can push back against the lies and disinformation that the MAGA Republicans are pushing."
 Democrats' struggles to reach Black, southern voters create frustration
 As Blavity previously reported, Nixon, a Democratic socialist, won an upset victory in Florida's Senate Democratic Primary this summer, defeating retired Lt. Col. Alex Vindman, who had the backing of much of the Democratic Party establishment. While Nixon's victory was part of a wave of socialist and other progressive candidates defeating centrists and establishment candidates in Democratic primaries, her general election campaign has reflected shortcomings within the party in terms of Black and southern voters. Atlanta Mayor Andre Dickens criticized the party earlier this year for ruling out hosting the 2028 Democratic National Convention in the city, calling this an example of the party's neglect for Black and southern voters. And a recent MS NOW report highlighted that hundreds of thousands of eligible Black voters had sat out recent elections in Ohio , with the Democratic Party failing to reach out to many potential Black voters in the state.

Raphael Warnock of Georgia recently called out the party for not doing more to support Black and southern candidates while he has personally sought to boost several of them during this election cycle. Warnock has especially pushed for more support for Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, as he challenges incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. Senate Majority PAC, a Democratic super PAC, only recently announced a $1.2 million ad campaign for Colom in the final weeks of the race. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Massachusetts) applauded the party for investing in Colom and in progressives like Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, but she argued that "we need to see more of that for Angie Nixon."
 With only days until the midterm election, the Democratic Party's issues with Black voters have increasingly surfaced in debate within the party. November's election results may hinge on how strongly Black voters turn out in the South and across the country, and the party's long-term success will largely rely on how well it mobilizes Black voters and supports Black candidates.
